description: We are a group of grad students from IF ITB looking to make an impact to Indonesia's wildfire management and countermeasures.
summary: Bara is a web application that turns more than two decades of NASA FIRMS active fire hotspots over Indonesia into one consistent burning activity calendar. MODIS and VIIRS see fires very differently: over Indonesia a VIIRS satellite records about seven hotspots for every Aqua MODIS hotspot, and the ratio changes with island group, season and time of day. Bara converts every VIIRS hotspot into Aqua MODIS-equivalent units using factors fitted by island group, month and day/night, giving one record from July 2002 to the present in which the sensor of origin no longer matters. Users pick a country, province or regency and see a daily calendar of burning, a map at about 5 km resolution, unusual months compared with the same month in other years, the weeks and months that are critical year after year, and a fire forecast from 30 days to 5 years ahead on the map timeline. Each fire event gets a suggested likely cause from forest loss, land cover, peat, rainfall and El Niño/IOD evidence. The record updates itself every hour, and anyone can subscribe to email alerts when their province or regency has an unusual month. It gives emergency responders, scientists and land managers a consistent, current picture for planning monitoring and response.
details:
What it does
- Harmonises MODIS (Terra, Aqua) and VIIRS (S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21) active fire detections into one unit: hotspots, Aqua MODIS-equivalent. An Aqua hotspot counts 1; a VIIRS hotspot counts 1/k, where ln k = base + island group effect + month effect, fitted separately for day and night because the VIIRS/MODIS ratio is about three times higher at night.
- Separates presumed vegetation fires from static sources (volcanoes, gas flares, industry) using a static-source mask built from the typed detections. Days with no satellite coverage are shown as missing, never as zero.
- Shows a burning activity calendar, map, time slider, fire events, sensor agreement view, monthly anomalies, historically critical months and weeks, and a fire forecast per 5 km cell (1 to 30 days, 1 to 12 months, 1 to 5 years) played on the map timeline. Any area can be exported as CSV.
- Suggests a likely cause for each fire event (land clearing, agricultural burning, wildfire or unknown) from Hansen forest loss, MODIS land cover, peatland, GPM IMERG rainfall and El Niño / Indian Ocean Dipole indices, with a confidence level and a clear disclaimer that this is related evidence, not proof of cause.
- Keeps itself current: an hourly job downloads new FIRMS data, rebuilds and checks the record, and only then publishes it.
- Email alerts: anyone can subscribe to up to 10 provinces or regencies and get an email when a month's fire activity there becomes unusual for that time of year, with double opt-in and one-click unsubscribe.

How we checked it
- Leave-one-year-out validation from 2012 to 2025: the harmonised VIIRS and Aqua monthly series correlate at r = 0.996 in log terms, with about 8% typical monthly difference and no overall bias. Every island group meets our pre-set convergence thresholds. A control comparing two identical VIIRS instruments (S-NPP against NOAA-20) gives r = 0.998.
- The forecast is evaluated on held-out years with Brier skill and AUC (the AUC for ranking which cells burn is 0.81 to 0.83).
- Critical periods match the reported fire seasons (for example August to October in Kalimantan and South Sumatra, and the second February-March season in the Riau Islands).
- Cause attribution follows the known geography of burning: agricultural burning leads in Java-Bali-Nusa Tenggara, land clearing in Sumatra, and wildfire in Kalimantan, Sulawesi-Maluku and Papua, with the 2015 and 2019 El Niño peat fires attributed to wildfire.
- Thresholds were fixed before fitting, and limits are documented openly, for example that the peak month differs in 3 of 14 years and that the forecast uses no weather inputs.

Impact
Fire managers in Indonesia can compare 2006, 2015, 2019 and 2023 on the same scale, see when a province's fire season usually starts, spot when the current month is out of the ordinary, and be told by email when it happens in their area.

Tools
Python, FastAPI, DuckDB, Parquet, NumPy and Rasterio for the data pipeline, context layers and API. TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL and Three.js for the dashboard and the 3D landing page. Pytest and Vitest for tests. Docker, Google Cloud Run, a Cloud Run job with Cloud Scheduler for hourly updates, and Cloud Storage for the data.

What makes it creative
Instead of showing two sensors side by side, it builds one statistically validated record, adds the context needed to ask why a fire burned, and keeps it live. It also explains its own method in plain language, both on an interactive scroll-driven landing page and in the dashboard.
